stem: A commodity trades at USD 100. The risk-free rate is 5%, storage costs are 2% of value per year and the convenience yield is 3% per year, all continuously compounded. The 6-month futures price is closest to:

rationale.A: Incorrect. 100.00 subtracts storage costs instead of adding them, so the net carry becomes zero.
rationale.B: Incorrect. 103.56 ignores the convenience yield and uses only r + u.
rationale.C: Incorrect. 105.13 adds the convenience yield to the carry; it should reduce the forward price.
rationale.D: Correct. The net carry is 5% + 2% − 3% = 4% a year, applied for half a year.

stem: Copper trades at USD 70 per unit spot and the 1-year futures price is USD 68. The risk-free rate is 5% and storage costs are 1% of value per year, both continuously compounded. The implied convenience yield is closest to:

rationale.B: Incorrect. 7.90% leaves out the 1% storage cost.
rationale.C: Incorrect. 3.10% adds ln(68/70) instead of subtracting it, reversing the sign of the log term.
rationale.D: Incorrect. 2.90% is just −ln(F/S); it ignores the interest and storage that the convenience yield must offset.

stem: The futures curve for natural gas slopes downward: longer-dated contracts trade below the spot price. Which explanation is most consistent with this shape?
options: Storage costs are unusually high relative to interest rates
The convenience yield exceeds the sum of the risk-free rate and storage costs
Inventories are plentiful, so holding gas offers little benefit
Futures prices exceed the expected future spot price
explanation: F = S e^((r + u − y)T) is below S only when y > r + u. A large convenience yield, usually caused by tight inventories, produces backwardation.

rationale.A: Incorrect. High storage costs push futures prices above spot, producing contango.
rationale.B: Correct. Backwardation requires the convenience yield to outweigh interest plus storage.
rationale.C: Incorrect. Plentiful inventories mean a low convenience yield, which is associated with contango.
rationale.D: Incorrect. That describes contango relative to expected spot, not a futures curve below the current spot price.

stem: For crude oil, the observed 1-year futures price is well below (S + U)e^(rT), where U is the present value of storage costs. Which statement is most accurate?
options: A riskless profit is available by selling oil from inventory and buying futures, and refiners will do so
The futures price must be wrong because the cost-of-carry relationship holds as an equality for all commodities
This is consistent with no-arbitrage because oil is a consumption commodity whose holders value physical inventory
A riskless profit is available by buying spot oil, storing it and selling futures
explanation: For consumption commodities only the upper bound is enforced. Holders keep oil for production, so they will not sell inventory to exploit a low futures price; the gap is the convenience yield.

rationale.A: Incorrect. Refiners hold oil to keep plants running and generally will not sell inventory for this trade.
rationale.B: Incorrect. The equality holds for investment commodities such as gold, not for consumption commodities.
rationale.C: Correct. A futures price below full carry simply implies a positive convenience yield.
rationale.D: Incorrect. Cash-and-carry profits only when the futures price is above full carry; here it would lose money.
